notes.meaning: Moses is sent back to Pharaoh with the Lord's clear demand to release Israel so they can worship Him. God calls Himself the God of the Hebrews, reminding the king that these enslaved people belong to God, not Egypt. True freedom is given so that God's people may serve Him.

God warns Pharaoh that continuing to hold Israel back will bring a deadly disease on Egypt's livestock in the open fields. This judgment targeted animals prized for transport, farm work, and war, including horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep. Since the Egyptians worshipped several of these animals, the plague struck at both their wealth and their false gods.

The Lord promises to make a clear separation between the animals of Israel and those of Egypt. Even though their herds grazed nearby, not a single animal belonging to the Israelites would die. This miraculous protection proved that the coming disaster was not an ordinary sickness, but a direct act of God.

God sets a specific time for the plague, announcing that it will happen the very next day. Setting an exact appointment showed that the Lord holds complete control over nature and time. It also gave Pharaoh one last chance to turn from his stubbornness before the blow fell.

The next day, the disease struck just as God had promised, killing a vast number of Egyptian livestock in the fields. At the same time, not a single animal owned by the Israelites died. This devastating loss showed that Egypt's sacred cattle could neither protect themselves nor their owners against the living God.

Pharaoh sent messengers to check on the Israelites and discovered that not one of their animals had died. Even with clear proof of God's miraculous distinction, the king's heart remained heavy and unyielding. Pride blinded him to the obvious hand of God, and he refused to let the people go.

God commands Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of soot from a furnace and have Moses toss it toward the sky in front of Pharaoh. The soot would miraculously turn into fine dust spreading across the entire land, causing painful, inflamed boils on both humans and animals. Since furnaces and brick kilns were symbols of Israel's bitter enslavement, God turned the very tool of their oppression into a source of punishment for Egypt.

Moses and Aaron obey the command by gathering ashes and standing before Pharaoh. When Moses throws the soot into the air, open sores and burning boils immediately erupt on people and animals across Egypt. This plague came without any prior warning, striking directly at human bodies for the first time.

The court magicians could not even stand before Moses because they were covered in painful boils just like the rest of the Egyptians. Their secret arts and prayers to their healing gods were completely useless to protect themselves or help others. They were utterly humiliated and forced to retreat from the royal court.

For the first time in the plague narrative, Scripture states that the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart. After Pharaoh had repeatedly hardened himself against earlier warnings, God confirmed him in his stubborn rebellion. As a result, the king refused to listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the Lord had foretold.

differ.view: God actively and sovereignly hardened Pharaoh's heart according to His eternal decree to demonstrate His justice.
God gave Pharaoh over to his own chosen rebellion after he repeatedly hardened his own heart against God's grace.

notes.meaning: God commands Moses to rise early in the morning and confront Pharaoh once again with the same demand to let His people go so they may worship Him. The constant repetition showed God's unchanging will and left Pharaoh without any excuse for his continued defiance.

The Lord warns Pharaoh that He will now send a series of heavier plagues aimed directly at the king's own heart and his people. These upcoming strikes would cut deeper than mere property losses, shaking Pharaoh's inner life with terror. God's purpose was to prove beyond question that there is no other god like Him in all the earth.

God explains that He could easily have wiped Pharaoh and his nation off the earth with a single deadly disease by now. His restraint showed that Egypt survived only because God chose to spare them, not because Pharaoh had any power to resist.

God reveals that He kept Pharaoh alive on the throne for a specific purpose: to display divine power through him and cause God's name to be proclaimed across the entire world. Pharaoh thought he was ruling Egypt by his own strength, but God was using the king's defiance to make His own glory known to all nations.

differ.view: God raised up Pharaoh to display His sovereign power and justice in the destruction of an obstinate rebel.
God kept Pharaoh standing alive despite his rebellion so that divine power might be seen and His name proclaimed.

notes.meaning: God confronts Pharaoh for still setting himself up as an obstacle against His people by refusing to let them go. The king acted like a high rampart blocking Israel's path, but fighting against God's people was really an act of war against God Himself.

The Lord announces that at the exact same hour tomorrow, He will send the most destructive hailstorm Egypt had ever experienced since its founding. Thunderstorms and hail were extremely rare and terrifying in Egypt's dry climate. Giving an exact time proved that the elements obeyed the Creator rather than Egypt's sky gods.

In great mercy, God gives Pharaoh and his people a practical warning to bring all outdoor workers and livestock inside to safety. Anything left in the open fields would be struck down and killed by the falling hail. Even in the middle of fierce judgment, God provided a way of escape for anyone willing to listen.

Some of Pharaoh's officials took the warning seriously and hurried their servants and livestock into shelter, while others showed contempt for God's word and left everything outside. This moment divided the Egyptians based on whether they feared the Lord's warning. Believing God's word brought life and safety, while ignoring it brought ruin.

When the time arrives, the Lord instructs Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven so hail will fall over the entire land. This gesture showed that the judgment came directly from the God of heaven above, not from earthly magic. The storm would strike people, animals, and vegetation alike across Egypt.

Moses lifts his staff toward the sky, and the Lord unleashes deafening thunder, heavy hail, and lightning that ran along the ground like fiery torches. It was a miraculous and unnatural combination of ice and blazing fire working together to execute God's judgment. Nothing so terrifying had ever struck Egypt in all its history.

The storm wreaked terrible destruction everywhere outside, killing every person and animal left exposed in the fields. The huge hailstones also battered down crops and tore limbs off the trees. Everything left unprotected suffered under the force of the storm.

The only place in all Egypt without hail was the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived. God drew a clear line of protection around His people while judgment fell all around them. This miraculous difference showed that the Lord cares for His own and has power to protect them in any crisis.

Terrified by the deadly storm, Pharaoh quickly summons Moses and Aaron and confesses that he has sinned. He admits that the Lord is completely righteous and that he and his people are in the wrong. While his words sounded like genuine repentance, he was mainly terrified of the destruction rather than truly broken over his sin.

Pharaoh begs Moses to pray to the Lord to stop the mighty thunder and hail, promising that he will finally let the people go. He had heard enough of the terrifying storm and agreed to make no more delays. Panic pushed him to make promises he had no real heart to keep once the danger passed.

Moses agrees to leave the city and lift up his hands in prayer so the storm will cease. This answer to prayer would show Pharaoh that the entire earth belongs to the Lord, not just Egypt's local gods. True worship belongs to the One who rules both heaven and earth.

Moses speaks with remarkable courage, telling Pharaoh plainly that neither he nor his officials yet have a true, lasting fear of God. Moses knew the king's confession was driven only by momentary panic rather than heartfelt obedience.

These verses explain that the flax and barley were completely ruined because the barley was already in the ear and the flax was in bloom. In contrast, the wheat and spelt were spared because they ripened later and were still supple beneath the ground. This detailed note shows that God gave Egypt a remaining mercy and another chance to turn before all their food was gone.

Moses walks out of the city into the open storm, completely confident of God's protection, and spreads out his hands in prayer. At his intercession, the thunder, hail, and torrential rain immediately stop. God showed His supreme power by commanding the storm to cease the moment His servant prayed.

As soon as the rain, hail, and thunder stopped, Pharaoh went back on his word and sinned even more. He and his court officials hardened their hearts again, refusing to let the Israelites leave. In the end, Pharaoh's stubbornness fulfilled exactly what the Lord had told Moses from the beginning.
